sentence: She have been working here since March.
options: She has been working here since March.
She have worked here since March.
She been working here since March.
She has been work here since March.
answer: She has been working here since March.
explanation: With he, she or it, use 'has', not 'have'. 'She has been working' is the correct present perfect continuous.

sentence: I am agree with your opinion.
options: I agree with your opinion.
I am agreeing with your opinion.
I am agree to your opinion.
I agreed with your opinion yesterday.
answer: I agree with your opinion.
explanation: 'Agree' is a verb, not an adjective, so it does not need 'am'. Say 'I agree', never 'I am agree'.

sentence: He don't like spicy food.
options: He doesn't like spicy food.
He don't likes spicy food.
He not like spicy food.
He didn't liked spicy food.
answer: He doesn't like spicy food.
explanation: With he, she or it, the negative of the present simple is 'doesn't', not 'don't'.

sentence: They is going to the market later.
options: They are going to the market later.
They be going to the market later.
They going to the market later.
They is go to the market later.
answer: They are going to the market later.
explanation: 'They' is plural, so the verb must be 'are'.

sentence: I went to the store and buy some eggs.
options: I went to the store and bought some eggs.
I go to the store and bought some eggs.
I went to the store and buying some eggs.
I gone to the store and buy some eggs.
answer: I went to the store and bought some eggs.
explanation: When two actions happened in the past in one sentence, keep the tense consistent: 'went' and 'bought'.

sentence: She is very good in mathematics.
options: She is very good at mathematics.
She is very good on mathematics.
She is very good with mathematics.
She is very good to mathematics.
answer: She is very good at mathematics.
explanation: The fixed phrase is 'good at' a subject or skill. Compare 'good in bed', 'good for you' — different prepositions change the meaning entirely.

sentence: My father is a honest man.
options: My father is an honest man.
My father is a honestly man.
My father is the honest man.
My father is an honestly man.
answer: My father is an honest man.
explanation: Use 'an' before a vowel SOUND, not just a vowel letter. 'Honest' starts with a silent 'h', so the first sound is a vowel.

sentence: We discussed about the plan yesterday.
options: We discussed the plan yesterday.
We discussed on the plan yesterday.
We discussed for the plan yesterday.
We were discussed the plan yesterday.
answer: We discussed the plan yesterday.
explanation: 'Discuss' already includes the idea of 'about' — you discuss something, not discuss about something. ('Talk about' is fine.)

sentence: The weather is more better today.
options: The weather is better today.
The weather is more good today.
The weather is most better today.
The weather is much more better today.
answer: The weather is better today.
explanation: 'Better' is already a comparative, so 'more better' doubles it up. You can say 'much better' to strengthen it.

sentence: I look forward to meet you next week.
options: I look forward to meeting you next week.
I look forward to meet you soon.
I am look forward to meeting you next week.
I looking forward to meet you next week.
answer: I look forward to meeting you next week.
explanation: After the preposition 'to' in 'look forward to', use the -ing form: 'look forward to meeting'.

sentence: There is many reasons to learn English.
options: There are many reasons to learn English.
There is much reasons to learn English.
There are much reasons to learn English.
There be many reasons to learn English.
answer: There are many reasons to learn English.
explanation: 'Reasons' is plural, so 'there are' is needed. Match the verb to the noun that follows it.

sentence: She said me that she was tired.
options: She told me that she was tired.
She said to that she was tired.
She told to me that she was tired.
She say me that she was tired.
answer: She told me that she was tired.
explanation: You 'tell someone' but 'say something to someone'. 'She said me' is wrong; either 'She told me' or 'She said to me' works.

sentence: I am living here since 2015.
options: I have been living here since 2015.
I am live here since 2015.
I lived here since 2015 being now.
I am living here for 2015.
answer: I have been living here since 2015.
explanation: For something that started in the past and continues now, use the present perfect (continuous): 'I have been living here since 2015'.

sentence: He suggested me to take a rest.
options: He suggested that I take a rest.
He suggested me take a rest.
He suggested me a rest to take.
He suggested to me take a rest.
answer: He suggested that I take a rest.
error: suggested me to → suggested that I
explanation: 'Suggest' never takes the pattern 'suggest someone to do'. Use 'suggest that someone do something' or 'suggest doing something'.

sentence: Despite of the rain, we enjoyed the trip.
options: Despite the rain, we enjoyed the trip.
Despite of the rain, we enjoy the trip.
Despite the rain, we have enjoyed the trip.
In despite of the rain, we enjoyed the trip.
answer: Despite the rain, we enjoyed the trip.
explanation: 'Despite' never takes 'of'. 'In spite of' does. So: 'Despite the rain' or 'In spite of the rain'.

sentence: If I would have known, I would have come earlier.
options: If I had known, I would have come earlier.
If I would know, I would have come earlier.
If I have known, I would come earlier.
If I had known, I would come earlier.
answer: If I had known, I would have come earlier.
explanation: In the if-clause of a third conditional, use the past perfect ('had known'), never 'would have'.

sentence: The teacher gave us many homeworks.
options: The teacher gave us a lot of homework.
The teacher gave us many homework.
The teacher gave us much homeworks.
The teacher gave us a homework.
answer: The teacher gave us a lot of homework.
error: many homeworks → a lot of homework
explanation: 'Homework' is uncountable, so it has no plural and never takes 'many'. Use 'a lot of homework' or 'much homework'.

sentence: I go to home after work every day.
options: I go home after work every day.
I go to house after work every day.
I went to home after work every day.
I go at home after work every day.
answer: I go home after work every day.
explanation: 'Home' works as an adverb in this phrase, so no preposition is needed: 'go home', not 'go to home'.

sentence: She is married with a doctor.
options: She is married to a doctor.
She is married of a doctor.
She married with a doctor.
She is marry to a doctor.
answer: She is married to a doctor.
explanation: The correct preposition after 'married' is 'to': 'married to someone'.

sentence: I did not went to the party last night.
options: I did not go to the party last night.
I did not gone to the party last night.
I not went to the party last night.
I do not went to the party last night.
answer: I did not go to the party last night.
explanation: After 'did' or 'did not', always use the base form of the verb: 'did not go'.

sentence: Each of the students have a laptop.
options: Each of the students has a laptop.
Each of the students have laptops.
Each of the student have a laptop.
Each the students has a laptop.
answer: Each of the students has a laptop.
explanation: 'Each' is always singular, so it takes 'has'. This is a very common trap because 'students' sits nearby.

sentence: She explained me the problem.
options: She explained the problem to me.
She explained to me the problem slowly.
She explained me about the problem.
She explain the problem to me.
answer: She explained the problem to me.
error: explained me → explained the problem to me
explanation: 'Explain' does not take an indirect object. You cannot 'explain someone something' — you explain something TO someone.

sentence: I have seen him yesterday at the library.
options: I saw him yesterday at the library.
I have saw him yesterday at the library.
I see him yesterday at the library.
I had seen him yesterday at the library.
answer: I saw him yesterday at the library.
explanation: The present perfect ('have seen') is never used with a finished past time like 'yesterday'. Use the simple past: 'saw'.

sentence: Neither the manager nor the workers was informed.
options: Neither the manager nor the workers were informed.
Neither the manager nor the workers is informed.
Neither the manager or the workers was informed.
Neither the manager nor the workers be informed.
answer: Neither the manager nor the workers were informed.
explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearest subject. 'Workers' is plural, so 'were' is correct.

sentence: He is capable to solve this problem.
options: He is capable of solving this problem.
He is capable to solving this problem.
He is capable solve this problem.
He is capable for solving this problem.
answer: He is capable of solving this problem.
explanation: The phrase is 'capable of doing' something. Compare 'able to do', which looks similar but takes 'to'.

sentence: This book is more interesting than that one is.
options: This book is more interesting than that one.
This book is more interesting that that one.
This book is much interesting than that one.
This book is interestinger than that one.
answer: This book is more interesting than that one.
explanation: In modern English, drop the final verb after 'than' when comparing two things directly: 'than that one', not 'than that one is'.

sentence: Hardly he had entered the room when the phone rang.
options: Hardly had he entered the room when the phone rang.
Hardly he entered the room when the phone had rang.
Hardly did he enter the room when the phone rang.
Hardly he has entered the room when the phone rang.
answer: Hardly had he entered the room when the phone rang.
error: Hardly he had → Hardly had he
explanation: When 'hardly', 'scarcely' or 'no sooner' starts the sentence, the subject and auxiliary verb swap places: 'Hardly HAD he entered'.

sentence: The number of students are increasing every year.
options: The number of students is increasing every year.
The number of students are increase every year.
A number of students is increasing every year.
The numbers of students are increasing every year.
answer: The number of students is increasing every year.
explanation: 'The number of' is treated as singular ('is'), while 'a number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb. This classic trap appears in exams constantly.

sentence: I would rather you don't tell anyone about this.
options: I would rather you didn't tell anyone about this.
I would rather you not tell anyone about this.
I would rather you don't told anyone about this.
I would rather you won't tell anyone about this.
answer: I would rather you didn't tell anyone about this.
explanation: After 'would rather' referring to another person, use the past tense: 'I would rather you didn't'.

sentence: He is one of the best player in the team.
options: He is one of the best players in the team.
He is one of the best player of the team.
He is one of best players in the team.
He is the one of the best player in the team.
answer: He is one of the best players in the team.
explanation: After 'one of the', the noun must be plural: 'one of the best players'. He is one member of a group of best players.

sentence: I look forward for your reply.
options: I look forward to your reply.
I look forward at your reply.
I am looking forward for your reply.
I look forward on your reply.
answer: I look forward to your reply.
explanation: 'Look forward to' is a fixed phrase. It is one of the most useful email closings in formal English.

sentence: She had better to see a doctor soon.
options: She had better see a doctor soon.
She had better to seeing a doctor soon.
She would better see a doctor soon.
She has better see a doctor soon.
answer: She had better see a doctor soon.
explanation: 'Had better' is followed directly by the base verb: 'had better see'. Despite the word 'had', it refers to advice about now or the future.

sentence: The concert was cancelled because the singer was sick, isn't it?
options: The concert was cancelled because the singer was sick, wasn't it?
The concert was cancelled because the singer was sick, didn't it?
The concert was cancelled because the singer was sick, was it?
The concert was cancelled because the singer was sick, is it?
answer: The concert was cancelled because the singer was sick, wasn't it?
explanation: A question tag matches the main verb in tense and polarity: 'was cancelled ... wasn't it?' Note that 'isn't it' is used very loosely in some dialects, but standard English requires the match.

sentence: I am boring in this class.
options: I am bored in this class.
I am boring of this class.
I am boring from this class.
I feel boring in this class.
answer: I am bored in this class.
explanation: 'Bored' describes how you feel; 'boring' describes what causes the feeling. If you say 'I am boring', you are saying you are a dull person.

sentence: We have been waiting since two hours.
options: We have been waiting for two hours.
We have been waiting from two hours.
We are waiting since two hours.
We have been waiting during two hours.
answer: We have been waiting for two hours.
explanation: 'For' goes with a length of time (two hours), 'since' with a starting point (since 3 p.m.).

sentence: She didn't said anything during the meeting.
options: She didn't say anything during the meeting.
She didn't says anything during the meeting.
She not said anything during the meeting.
She didn't speaking anything during the meeting.
answer: She didn't say anything during the meeting.
explanation: After 'didn't', use the base form: 'didn't say'.

sentence: It depends of the weather.
options: It depends on the weather.
It depends to the weather.
It is depend on the weather.
It depends at the weather.
answer: It depends on the weather.
explanation: The phrase is 'depend on'. 'Depends of' is a direct translation trap from several European languages.

sentence: If it will rain tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
options: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
If it will rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
If it rain tomorrow, we would cancel the picnic.
If it rained tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
answer: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
explanation: In a first conditional, the if-clause uses the present simple, never 'will'. The 'will' goes in the result clause.

sentence: She has been to Paris last summer.
options: She went to Paris last summer.
She has gone to Paris last summer.
She has been to Paris on last summer.
She was being to Paris last summer.
answer: She went to Paris last summer.
explanation: A finished time expression like 'last summer' requires the simple past: 'went'. The present perfect needs an open time frame.

sentence: He is interested to learn about history.
options: He is interested in learning about history.
He is interested to learning about history.
He is interested on learning about history.
He is interesting in learning about history.
answer: He is interested in learning about history.
explanation: 'Interested in' + -ing form is the correct pattern. A person is 'interested'; a book or topic is 'interesting'.

sentence: The informations you gave me were very useful.
options: The information you gave me was very useful.
The informations you gave me was very useful.
The information you gave me were very useful.
The informations you gave me were very useful.
answer: The information you gave me was very useful.
explanation: 'Information' is uncountable: no plural, and it takes a singular verb. The same goes for advice, news, research and luggage.

sentence: I forgot my phone in the office.
options: I left my phone in the office.
I forget my phone in the office.
I forgotten my phone in the office.
I was forgetting my phone in the office.
answer: I left my phone in the office.
explanation: For leaving something behind in a place, English uses 'left', not 'forgot'. 'I forgot my phone' means you forgot that it exists.

sentence: She is used to wake up early.
options: She is used to waking up early.
She used to waking up early.
She is use to wake up early.
She is used to wake up early every day.
answer: She is used to waking up early.
explanation: 'Be used to' means 'be accustomed to' and takes the -ing form. Compare 'used to wake up early', which describes a past habit and needs no 'be'.

sentence: Although it was late, but we decided to continue.
options: Although it was late, we decided to continue.
Although it was late, so we decided to continue.
Although it was late, however we decided to continue.
Although it was late, and we decided to continue.
answer: Although it was late, we decided to continue.
explanation: In English, one linking word is enough. 'Although' already does the job of 'but', so pairing them is a classic error in spoken and written English.

sentence: Can you borrow me your pen?
options: Can you lend me your pen?
Can you borrow me your pencil?
Can you lent me your pen?
Can you loan me your pen for borrow?
answer: Can you lend me your pen?
explanation: The owner 'lends'; the receiver 'borrows'. 'Borrow me' is wrong — you borrow FROM someone.

sentence: He speaks English more fluent than me.
options: He speaks English more fluently than me.
He speaks English more fluent than I.
He speaks English fluenter than me.
He speaks English most fluently than me.
answer: He speaks English more fluently than me.
explanation: You need an adverb to describe HOW he speaks, and adverbs are compared with 'more': 'more fluently'.

sentence: One of my friend lives in Sabah.
options: One of my friends lives in Sabah.
One of my friend live in Sabah.
One of my friends live in Sabah.
One my friends lives in Sabah.
answer: One of my friends lives in Sabah.
explanation: After 'one of', use the plural ('friends'), but the verb stays singular because the subject is 'one': 'one of my friends lives'.

sentence: I have finished the report yesterday evening.
options: I finished the report yesterday evening.
I have finish the report yesterday evening.
I had finished the report yesterday evening.
I have been finishing the report yesterday evening.
answer: I finished the report yesterday evening.
explanation: 'Yesterday evening' is finished past time, so the simple past is required. Present perfect needs open time like 'this week' or 'recently'.

sentence: The meeting is in Monday morning.
options: The meeting is on Monday morning.
The meeting is at Monday morning.
The meeting is in Monday at morning.
The meeting is for Monday morning.
answer: The meeting is on Monday morning.
explanation: Days and dates take 'on' (on Monday), months and years take 'in' (in May), and clock times take 'at' (at 9 a.m.).

sentence: Everybody in this class speak English very well.
options: Everybody in this class speaks English very well.
Everybody in this class speaking English very well.
Everybody in this class are speaking English very well.
Everybody in this class speak English very good.
answer: Everybody in this class speaks English very well.
explanation: 'Everybody', 'everyone', 'nobody' and 'someone' are grammatically singular and take -s on the verb.
